newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan voices concern about US bank reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan voices concern about US bank reform bill.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan voiced concern on Thursday about a bill to reform U.S. financial laws, although he said he supported the "overall thrust" of the proposed legislation.

In prepared testimony to a House Commerce subcommittee, the central bank chief said the bill, already approved by the House Banking Committee, went too far in allowing banks to own or be owned by commercial companies.

While the Fed recognizes that the line between banking and commerce is already eroding and eventually will disappear, it thinks that regulators should move cautiously in knocking down the legal barriers that now separate the two, Greenspan said.

The proposed legislation, which narrowly passed the House Banking Committee, would allow banks to derive 15 percent of their revenue from commercial activities, and vice versa, subject to certain limits.
The bill "goes well beyond what both commercial banks and non-financial firms need to meet the requirements of today, as well as in the forseeable future," Greenspan said.

The legislation would also expand access to the Fed's electronic wire transfer network, which Greenspan termed a "linchpin" of the international monetary system. "Disruptions and disturbances in the U.S. payment system thus can easily have global implications," he said.
That makes it all the more important for the Fed to continue to have a premier role in overseeing financial holding companies that are major players in the banking system, the Fed chief argued.

"We believe that the central bank's role in the prevention and containment of financial crises and as guarantor of the payment system requires that we continue to have a consolidated oversight responsibility for most holding companies," he said.
The bill coming out the Banking Committee "appropriately recognizes this," he added.

However, he took issue with provisions in the bill allowing banks to conduct non-banking activities in direct subsidiaries. Greenspan has long argued that such activities should be conducted in separate affiliates of bank holding companies.
